unesco.title: Morna, musical practice of Cabo Verde
unesco.description: Morna, musical practice of Cabo Verde is a traditional Cape Verdean musical and choreographic practice with instrumental accompaniment that incorporates voice, music, poetry, and dance. Morna can be either sung or played only with instruments, mainly chordophones, including the guitar, violin, ten-string guitar, replaced with a cavaquinho in the twentieth century, and the ukulele. Several other instruments have now been introduced – such as the piano, percussion and bass – but the guitar remains the preferred instrument. The lyric poetry can be improvised, with topics including love, departure, separation, reunion, longing, the ocean and the motherland. While in the past the lyrics were also composed in Portuguese, nowadays it is mainly composed in Cape Verdean Creole. Bearers and practitioners of the element include instrument players, singers, poets, and composers, who perform, disseminate and transmit the practice to the younger generations. Currently, some bearers are also opening teaching centres, and as a genre Morna is also practised by formal groups. Morna is a fundamental aspect of Cape Verdean social and cultural life, as it performed at key life events, such as weddings, christenings, and family reunions. Transmission has been carried out by the community, through workshops, radio programmes, performances, festivals, and the musical contest entitled ‘Todo Mundo Canta’, which takes place on every island.

profile.name: morna
profile.tagline: Cape Verde's national ballroom dance of slow sorrow, romance, and ocean longing.
profile.insight: In a Cape Verdean morna, a couple sways together twice to one side per bar, mirroring the melancholic pull of the ocean and the painful departure for foreign shores.
profile.profile: The morna is the national music and ballroom dance of Cape Verde, characterized by a slow tempo, binary meter, and themes of saudade, love, and separation. Performed in pairs with a gentle embracing arm and hand-hold, dancers execute two synchronized body swings to one side per bar, shifting to the opposite side on the next. The genre blends acoustic instrumentation like the guitar, violin, and cavaquinho, and was proclaimed an UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2019.
profile.profile_long:
The morna is a traditional Cape Verdean musical and choreographic practice that serves as a fundamental aspect of the nation's social and cultural life. Historically, the dance emerged as a ballroom genre, performed in pairs with a specific, intimate embrace: one arm encircles the partner, while the other hand holds the partner's hand. The movement is characterized by a rhythmic sway, with the couple executing two body swings to one side within a single bar of music, before shifting to the opposite side in the following bar. This physical movement mirrors the slow, melancholic, and romantic nature of the music, which is deeply rooted in the concept of 'saudade'—a profound longing for home, loved ones, or the sea.

The musical structure of the morna is traditionally built on a cycle of fifths, though modern compositions have introduced more complex harmonic variations. It is typically performed in a binary meter with a lento tempo. The instrumentation is predominantly acoustic, featuring the guitar (violão) as the primary instrument, often accompanied by the cavaquinho, violin (rabeca), piano, clarinet, or accordion. The vocal style is emotive, with lyrics frequently composed in Cape Verdean Creole, exploring themes of love, departure, separation, and the motherland. 

Origins of the morna are traced back to the 18th century on Boa Vista Island, though it matured significantly in the 20th century. Poet and composer Eugénio Tavares is credited with introducing the intense lyricism and romanticism that define the genre today, particularly through the Brava style. Later, in the 1930s and 1940s, the São Vicente style emerged, incorporating 'passing chords'—a technique popularized by B. Leza that enriched the harmonic progression beyond the traditional cycle of fifths. 

Today, the morna remains a living tradition, performed at significant life events such as weddings, christenings, and family reunions. It is transmitted through community workshops, festivals, and radio programs. Internationally, the genre gained significant recognition through the performances of artists such as Cesária Évora, who brought the 'saudade' of Cape Verde to global stages. While the dance is a social ballroom practice, it is deeply embedded in the identity of the Cape Verdean people, serving as a bridge between the islands and the diaspora.

sections.origins_and_history: The morna originated in the 18th century on Boa Vista Island. It is believed to be a cross between the lundum and the choros. In the early 20th century, Eugénio Tavares introduced a more romantic and lyrical style in Brava. During the 1930s and 1940s, B. Leza introduced 'passing chords' in São Vicente, enriching the harmonic structure.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The morna is a ballroom dance performed in pairs. Dancers embrace their partner with one arm and hold hands with the other. The movement consists of two body swings to one side per bar, with the direction of the swing alternating every bar.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is typically lento with a binary meter. Traditional instrumentation includes the guitar (violão), cavaquinho, violin (rabeca), piano, clarinet, and accordion. The harmonic structure often follows a cycle of fifths, though passing chords are used in some regional variants.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The morna is performed at key life events such as weddings, christenings, and family reunions. It is a symbol of national identity, reflecting themes of saudade, love, departure, and the sea.
sections.notable_figures: Cesária Évora, Eugénio Tavares, B. Leza, Bana, and Fantcha.
sections.regional_variants: Boa Vista morna (quicker tempo, rubato style), Brava morna (slower tempo, romanticism, rigid meter), and São Vicente morna (enriched chord sequences with passing chords).
sections.lineage: The morna is related to the lundum and the choros, and shares cultural connections with the Portuguese fado, Brazilian modinha, and Argentine tango.

basic_steps: Hold partner with one arm around waist and other hand held.
Sway body twice to the left side during one bar of music.
Sway body twice to the right side during the next bar of music.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Syncopated, with the melody accentuated on the first beat and the last half-beat of the bar.
music_profile.vocal_style: Emotive, lyrical, often in Cape Verdean Creole.
music_profile.sound_description: A slow, acoustic sound characterized by the interplay of guitar arpeggios and melodic solo instruments like the violin, conveying a sense of deep longing.

movement_profile.arms_and_hands: One arm around partner, other hand held.

signature_moves.name: Body sway
signature_moves.description: Two rhythmic swings of the body to one side per bar.

claims.text: The morna is a music and dance genre from Cape Verde, proclaimed Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2019.
claims.quote: The morna (pronunciation in both Portuguese and Cape Verdean Creole: [ˈmɔɾnɐ]) is a music and dance genre from Cape Verde. It was proclaimed Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO on December 11, 2019.

claims.text: The dance is performed in pairs with a specific embrace and hand-hold, involving two body swings per bar.
claims.quote: As a dance the morna is a ballroom dance, danced in pairs. The performers dance with an arm embracing the partner, while with the other arm they hold hands. The dancing is made through two body swings to one side in a music's bar, while in the next bar the swinging is to the other side.

claims.text: The morna is traditionally performed with acoustic instruments like the guitar, violin, and cavaquinho.
claims.quote: Morna can be either sung or played only with instruments, mainly chordophones, including the guitar, violin, ten-string guitar, replaced with a cavaquinho in the twentieth century, and the ukulele.

claims.text: The genre's themes often revolve around love, departure, and the longing known as saudade.
claims.quote: Besides universal subjects like love, typically Cape Verdean subjects are talked about, such as departure abroad, the return, the saudade, love for the homeland and the sea.

claims.text: Eugénio Tavares is credited with introducing the romantic character of the morna in the early 20th century.
claims.quote: In the beginning of the 20th century, the poet Eugénio Tavares was one of the main people responsible for giving morna the romantic character that it has today.

claims.text: The São Vicente variant of the morna is known for its enriched chord sequences using passing chords.
claims.quote: One of the main people responsible for this enrichment was the composer Francisco Xavier da Cruz (a.k.a. B.Leza) who under Brazilian music influence introduced the so-called passing chords
